rss_0_1792447727.title: Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adult
rss_0_1792447727.text:
A Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of ⁠190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast ⁠in south-eastern Kenya.

Prosecutors say Mackenzie and ⁠his Good News International Church organised ​a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the ⁠court rejected that argument.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. Many were severely decomposed, and only 26 of them were able to be identified.

Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

View image in fullscreen Kenyan high court judge Diana Kavedza Mochache on 19 October. Photograph: EPA

Mackenzie was in ​court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, ‌one of the co-accused.

He was silent, ‌staring into space before the ruling was handed down.

Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa high ‌court.

Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.

Speaking before the verdict, he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems … I was hoping for this particular day.”

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

View image in fullscreen A Kenyan national youth service officer talks to a woman while on guard at the entrance to the Mombasa law courts on Monday 19 October. Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Kenya’s president, William Ruto, said in 2023 that government agencies should have been ​able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.

People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene ⁠sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

View image in fullscreen Paul Mackenzie and his co-accused during their court appearance on 19 October. Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told ​police that his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police ​arrested him again in April 2023 and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.

Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles (30km) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

rss_1_1792447727.title: Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan
rss_1_1792447727.text:
A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.

Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.

Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.

The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”

Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.

The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.

The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.

Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.

After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.

The fighting in Sudan has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.

Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN, warned the security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.

She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”

AFP contributed to this report

rss_2_1792447727.title: Ebola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key services
rss_2_1792447727.text:
An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region.

It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.

The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia airbase, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.

“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.

In the meantime, Kenyans were “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.

Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.

“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”

The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.

“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.

The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with the demolition of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US has slashed programs across the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.

“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”

The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”

Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.

The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response had also been “weakened”, he said.

A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. Since then, seven close contacts have tested positive.

Patrick Amoth, the director-general for health, confirmed on Sunday the total number of ‌infections in the country was eight.

Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.

“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DR Congo and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.

A French doctor who returned from DR Congo in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DR Congo to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.

In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DR Congo and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.

Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican senator from Louisiana, penned a letter in June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.

Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts was “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and had “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.

“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.

Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.

Work such as HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests, the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”

rss_3_1792447727.title: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music
rss_3_1792447727.text:
For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.

His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.

View image in fullscreen Toby Shang by the waterfront in the Lagos suburb of Akoka. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

“Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.

Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.

Allow TikTok content? This article includes content provided by TikTok . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue

Hypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals “and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.

Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.

View image in fullscreen Toby Shang made a name for himself while still a student at the University of Lagos. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

“Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.

Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene include Deborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis – an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.

The art of hyping as it is known in west and central Africa has its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to The Long Wave Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

These styles laid the foundation for the atalaku (meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.

Exponents of this style include the American gospel singer Kirk Franklin as well as the Congolese rumba bandleader Koffi Olomide and the Congolese singer Awilo Longomba.

The success of Olomide and Longomba at the turn of the 21st century set off a craze in Côte d’Ivoire, where coupé-décalé music embraced the atalaku trend alongside farotement, the act of showing off by throwing cash at performers or guests at parties.

View image in fullscreen The Congolese singer Koffi Olomide performing at a festival in Abidjan in September 2021. Photograph: Sia Kambou/AFP/Getty

A line encouraging audiences to gallop like a horse in the Ivorian star DJ Arafat’s 2003 viral homage to a late friend – “Tout le monde galope, kirikata kirikata” – influenced later hits from Nigerian Afrobeats musicians Flavour N’abania and Skales.

Côte d’Ivoire’s national television network, RTI, ran an atalaku talent hunt for several years. Lili Djely, an Ivorian woman of Malian origin, won the 2006 edition with a mix of Ivorian nouchi and French, defeating men to take the crown. In recent years, an MC/hypeman of the year category was introduced at the Ghana DJ awards as hype flourished there too.

Allow TikTok content? This article includes content provided by TikTok . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue

Thanks to the success of Afrobeats, Afrohype is now widely recognised as a full-time career. As artists became more expensive to book after Covid-19, promoters turned to hypemen – previously criticised for simply doing voiceovers. Some are now reportedly paid as much as 5-8m naira (£2,844–4,550) for a 30-minute or one-hour performance.

Some observers, however, say hype is a nuisance, amping up noise levels at events or encouraging fraudulent lifestyles, and that many performers do not customise language and tempo to fit the event.

View image in fullscreen The Congolese musician Awilo Longomba performing at the All Africa music awards in Lagos in November 2019. Photograph: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP/Getty

Nevertheless, hypemen are now a permanent fixture on the entertainment scene. For Shang, they are helping fun-seekers and club-goers get back on the dancefloor.

“People are facing a lot of challenges … they need somebody to tell them money is coming in the new week,” he said. “Also, everybody wants to press their phones or show Birkin bags in clubs. Nobody wants to dance because dancing is seen as for small kids. You need a hypeman to bring out that childlike part in every person. A 60-year-old woman can start dancing like a young girl if the hype is good enough.”

rss_4_1792447728.title: An extraordinary life: descendant welcomes biography of woman ‘gifted’ to Queen Victoria
rss_4_1792447728.text:
When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s great-great-grandmother Sarah Forbes Bonetta was presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a “diplomatic gift” from an African king.

Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta’s education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa’s wealthiest men, and become godmother to her eldest daughter.

But while Victoria took a genuine interest in Bonetta’s welfare, making the orphan a royal protege and meeting with her over the years, their relationship was part of a bigger agenda.

Now, as a biography is published – Becoming Sarah Forbes Bonetta: A Yorùbá Woman in Queen Victoria’s Court – Randle has spoken of his family history.

“I don’t think a human being, who has agency, could be ‘gifted’ from one to another, but had she not been gifted to Queen Victoria, would I be here today?” said Randle, a British-Nigerian barrister from London.

View image in fullscreen Bayo Randle, Bonetta’s great-great-grandson, is a barrister in London. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

The new book, by a Canadian academic, Prof Henry Lovejoy, charts how Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron, which was set up to enforce the abolition of the transatlantic trade.

Born in 1843 in Òkè-Òdàn, south-west Nigeria, Bonetta was originally called Àìná. Her family was killed in 1848 when her town was attacked by King Ghezo of Dahomey’s forces.

Bonetta, then five, is believed to have been captured by the agodjié – the all-female regiment depicted in the Hollywood movie The Woman King – and held at King Ghezo’s court.

View image in fullscreen The book by Henry B Lovejoy. Photograph: supplied

In 1850, Forbes went to Dahomey – which is now Benin – to petition Ghezo to sign an anti-slavery treaty. The mission failed but Forbes asked Ghezo if he could take Bonetta to England.

Bonetta would go on to live a life of renown, becoming one of the most artistically represented and widely reported African women of her time. But she was never truly free.

Lovejoy’s book describes how, before Forbes arrived in England with her – giving her his own name and that of his ship, the Bonetta – he petitioned for her to be “the property of the crown”.

This meant Bonetta was “effectively indentured to Queen Victoria until age 19” under the post-abolition legal structures, Lovejoy said. Bonetta was then married off to James Pinson Labulo Davies, a merchant and philanthropist, of whom she would write: “I don’t feel a particle of love for him.”

Lovejoy’s research for the website liberatedafricans.org, developed with Kartikay Chadha, documents how, after abolition, more than 700,000 Africans “liberated” from enslavers were forced into indentures of up to 14 years “to pay for the cost of their own freedom” by governments including Britain’s.

Lovejoy claims Bonetta was at the elite end of this bonded labour system, “educated to be a missionary who would Christianise Africa”. In her lifetime her image was exploited as imperial iconography, promoting the idea that British colonialism of Africa was a “civilising mission”.

View image in fullscreen Bonetta was a famous figure in 19th-century England. Photograph: Alamy

Lovejoy, of the University of Colorado Boulder, said: “Sarah’s imagery was used to project the idea of the queen’s benevolence – at a time when ‘liberated’ Africans are being forced into indentures.”

Nonetheless, when Bonetta attended the 1858 wedding of Queen Victoria’s daughter, the Princess Royal, American abolitionists saw it as proof that Victoria, then the most powerful woman on Earth, believed in equality.

For Randle, a plaster bust of Bonetta sculpted in 1851 by Benedetto Pistrucci, the Royal Mint’s chief engraver, symbolises the story’s “duality”. Randle saw it last year after Lovejoy had tracked it down to a private family collection in his research.

“Who gets to see what their great ancestor looked like as a child, the cultural markings on her face? That is amazing. But at the same time it was a bust prepared for phrenological purposes, within a racist framework, where [Bonetta] was shown as an ‘excellent specimen’,” Randle said.

Randle first learned his family history from his father, Adekunle Randle, a retired lawyer. The family still has the engraved goblet and plate that Queen Victoria gave to Bonetta’s daughter, Victoria, who, with the queen’s help, was educated at Cheltenham ladies’ college.

Lovejoy’s book challenges the myths that Bonetta was a Yoruba princess, that she herself was Queen Victoria’s goddaughter, and that she spent most of her life in England.

Randle, 37, who maintains his family’s ancestral ties with Òkè-Òdàn, welcomes research into Bonetta, who was a gifted linguist, musician, travel writer, educator and leading woman in 19th-century Lagos, until her death from tuberculosis in Madeira in 1880, aged 37.

“Whether [Lovejoy’s] book is comfortable for me is beside the point,” Randle said. “It’s for the advancement of knowledge and how we learn from the past. Where the real discomfort lies is in what [Bonetta] was the symbol of, what she was used for.

“But it would be a mistake to paint her story as entirely tragic,” he added. “My great-great-grandmother was very capable, courageous and dignified through adversity – through the trauma of losing her family, being displaced, and changing like a chameleon to fit into a culture so alien from what she’d known, she thrived. She is an early example of Black Britain.”

rss_5_1792447728.title: Hurricane Trudy menaces Mexico’s Pacific coast and Greece hit by deadly floods
rss_5_1792447728.text:
In contrast to the quiet Atlantic hurricane season, there has been ongoing activity in the Pacific, with Trudy being the 22nd and latest named system. The category 2 hurricane remained roughly 100 miles (160km) south-west of the coast of Mexico, meaning the worst of the conditions stayed offshore. However, the US National Hurricane Center put coastal parts of the states of Jalisco, Michoacán and Colima under hurricane warnings, with sustained winds of up to 60-90mph forecast on Sunday.

Rainfall totals of 100-150mm were likely for these areas, prompting warnings of flooding and landslides. Warnings also covered the risk of a dangerous storm surge accompanied by damaging waves in areas of onshore winds across the coast of south-western Mexico. By Monday morning, Trudy had weakened and been downgraded to a tropical storm, with coastal warnings being lifted.

In Greece, heavy rain and thunderstorms caused severe flooding and one fatality across Rhodes, Evia and the Sporades islands last week. According to the National Observatory of Athens, a station in Rhodes recorded 202mm between 3.30am and 9.50am (UTC) on 14 October. Regional authorities reported more than 30 rescue and extrication operations in response to flooding, while the Greek coastguard said four passenger vehicles were swept into the sea during the storm. On Skiathos, flood waters swept away two cars.

View image in fullscreen Cars swept into the sea on the Greek island of Rhodes. Photograph: Kyriakos Finas/Reuters

Five deaths were reported due to severe flooding in Istanbul, Turkey, last week. Heavy rain on 14 and 15 October prompted school closures, flight delays, disruptive flooding and landslides across several provinces. According to the Istanbul metropolitan municipality, 242mm of rain was recorded in Beykoz, a district of Istanbul province. Nearly 600 people were rescued after becoming stranded and at least 2,700 people were forced to evacuate their homes.

The Turkish state meteorological service issued further alerts for heavy rain and thunderstorms over the weekend across dozens of provinces, with at least an additional 40-60mm forecast for parts of the Marmara and western Black Sea regions.

rss_6_1792447728.title: ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists
rss_6_1792447728.text:
Albertans are going to the polls to decide their place in Canada, in a referendum that has exposed deep divisions within the province, not least in the separatist movement itself.

On Monday, voters will respond to the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada, or hold a second, binding independence referendum.

A minority have long argued that separation is the only way to address their belief that Alberta is short-changed by its financial relationship with Ottawa, and prevented from fully exploiting the province’s vast fossil fuel reserves.

Any enthusiasm either side might have held headed into the referendum was muted after a deadly fire broke out at a major military base in the province. On Saturday afternoon, a blaze tore through the CFB Wainwright and into the nearby town. Canada’s armed forces announced with “profound sadness” that there had been multiple deaths and injuries.

The premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, argued for years that a referendum was not needed, but called one anyway after pressure from some within her United Conservative party.

View image in fullscreen Alberta’s premier, Danielle Smith, called a referendum after pressure from some within her United Conservative party. Photograph: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP

Nevertheless, Smith did not campaign in favour of independence, saying in June she estimated the cost of separating at about C$400bn (£212bn) for the transition and another $25bn-$50bn in annual costs associated with starting a new country. Smith’s caution prompted some of her supporters to accuse her of betraying the independence movement.

Opponents of independence have focused heavily on the costs of separation, with the University of Calgary’s school of public policy saying in June it could be up to $170bn over a five-year period and be highly unpredictable in the long term.

The issue has not divided neatly along partisan lines. The former premiers Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley – from the rightwing Conservative and leftwing New Democratic party – have appeared on stage together, setting aside a bitter ideological rivalry that more usually defines Albertan politics.

Mark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: to build a stronger Alberta and a greater Canada to leave for our children, or to burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty,” the prime minister told a raucous crowd.

Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, saw first-hand the effects of the Brexit vote and the economic upheaval that followed.

“This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities,” he said. “Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”

View image in fullscreen Mark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada. Photograph: Megan Albu/AFP/Getty Images

Carney, whom recent polls identify as the most popular politician in Alberta, joined the former deputy premier of Alberta Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for the latter’s Forever Canadian group. Lukaszuk has driven more than 40,000km (24,855 miles) around Alberta in a 1992 motorhome named the Unity Bus and distributed at least 100,000 lawn signs.

Rather than campaigning frequently, Carney has pointed to big projects his government is looking to move ahead with that would benefit the province, including a pipeline to the Pacific coast to increase the flow of Alberta crude oil to Asia.

“I won’t sugar-coat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” said Carney.

Energy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa, stemming from the 1980 national energy programme, which sought greater federal control over the energy sector, provoked fierce opposition in Alberta and helped erode Liberal support across western Canada. The sense that the province’s wealth was being siphoned eastward is older still: a 1915 cartoon, “The Milch Cow”, depicted Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba as farmers feeding a cow whose milk was funnelled into buckets labelled Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal.

“Growing up, I remember. I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” Carney told the crowd. “And more recently, we were made to feel that our energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

View image in fullscreen Energy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa. Photograph: Jeff McIntosh/AP

The movement seeking to capitalise on those grievances, however, has been marked by competing interests, personal rivalries and allegations surrounding some of its leading figures. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is alleged to have mismanaged millions of dollars of First Nations trust funds, while David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organiser, was at the centre of a voter-data scandal that exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation.

Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of the province’s modern separatist movement, recently published the Alberta transition plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning it into an independent country.

Rejecting comparisons to Brexit and the economic fallout, Wilson said: “Every single thing we found that needs to be addressed to do the transition is absolutely doable,” calling most of the tasks “super easy”.

Wilson dismissed the idea that negotiations between an independent Alberta and Canada’s federal government would be acrimonious and lengthy.

“It would be economic suicide for them to challenge Alberta,” he said. “You want to cut off trade with us? OK. By the way, go buy axes and chainsaws because you’re going to have to cut down all the maple trees to keep warm this winter because you’re not going to get our energy products.”

Even within the separatist camp, there are doubts about how quickly independence could be achieved. Bill Jones, a member of the Wildrose Independence party, said its leaders were moving too quickly without the institutions a new country would need, from a police force to a pension system.

View image in fullscreen Alberta flags flutter next to a banner calling for separation in rural Alberta. Photograph: Todd Korol/Reuters

“We – Alberta – were always meant to be a colony, to get resources that were here to go east,” said Jones. “And that mindset is still there.”

“I don’t see the evidence for our independence. If we go out today, we’d be a failed state for generations. The great-great-grandchildren would be still suffering. And that’s the problem.”

Monday’s referendum will also include nine other measures unrelated to separation, including proposals affecting social programmes, judicial appointments and the senate.

One remain campaign has distributed thousands of “no to the nine” lawn signs around the province. Even some separatists, angry at Smith, have started a “decline the 9” campaign. Smith, for her part, has pushed a “yes to the rest” message in response.

In Calgary, the city’s mayor said he was “duty bound” to speak out about the perils of an attempt to fracture the country.

“There will be catastrophic impacts that would arise from separation,” said Jeromy Farkas. “And the unfortunate bullshit implication of separation is that it’s invited a conversation about who is a ‘real Canadian’? Who is a ‘real Albertan’? If you are living here in Calgary, you are welcome here. We need to continue to signal that. We need to telegraph that stability.

“We stand to lose so much from simply even having this debate.”

In October, further details emerged about meetings between unelected Alberta separatists and both Republican operatives and staff at the US state department. Among items allegedly discussed were how oil royalties could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country. They also allegedly offered up Alberta’s fresh water resources.

No matter the results on Monday, the referendum could have looked far different if not for the intervention of First Nations, which successfully sued to force the Alberta government to either dismiss the question of separation or change the wording. Key to their argument was the fact that the land of modern-day Alberta is covered by five treaties signed with the crown before the creation of the province.

View image in fullscreen Protesters highlight concerns about Indigenous treaty rights and the broader implications of Alberta’s separation. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

The president of the Blackfoot Confederacy, Chief Troy “Bossman” Knowlton, said: “These treaties are living documents, but the ignorance of the separatists, and their bigotry, does not allow their mind to accept the fact that they’re not symbolic documents. They have power, and the reality is Alberta does not have the constitutional right to separate.”

Knowlton said that if separatists had proactively reached out to First Nations before pushing ahead with independence, it might have led to a different outcome. “But they treated us as a speed bump they could just drive over.”

He added that the First Nations’ legal victory was followed by what he viewed as recriminations from the province, including an unexplained halt to talks on land claims and cooperation with Alberta’s government.

“At the end of the day, we want Alberta to continue to be a beacon of light,” he said. “Because when the first newcomers came to these lands centuries ago, that’s what our chiefs said: we’ll share these resources we have here. So do we want prosperity for Alberta? You’d better believe it.”

rss_7_1792447728.title: Four people killed in ‘violent, fast-moving’ fire at Canadian military base
rss_7_1792447728.text:
Four people have been killed and dozens more seriously injured after a “violent, fast-moving” fire tore through one of Canada’s busiest military training bases in Alberta, the country’s prime minister said on Sunday.

Mark Carney called the incident “one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime”.

Winds up to 96km/h (60mph) fed the blaze, which broke out at 4pm on Saturday during high-intensity combat training at the base. Alberta premier Danielle Smith said at a press conference on Sunday evening that 39 people were in hospital after the fire, with at least 19 of them in a critical condition.

Maj Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said that a grass fire ignited in a training area of the military base, which spread quickly. The cause of the fire was being investigated, he said.

The military identified those killed as Sgt Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light infantry. All four were serving with the battalion, based in Edmonton.

Rutland said military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained before winds suddenly shifted, sending flames racing toward the soldiers.

“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 36 seconds,” he said at a news conference in Edmonton.

“I’ve certainly never seen anything like it,” he added.

The fire broke out during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light infantry, sweeping into the area where the simulated attacks were taking place.

About 84 soldiers were in the company, which was split between a grenade range and an area where soldiers practised attacks on simulated enemy positions.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost. And I have asked the flags on all federal buildings to be flown at half-mast to honour them,” Carney told the nation in an address from Ottawa. “We are praying for the wounded.”

Carney said he had requested a “detailed account” from military officials on the ground about what had happened.

View image in fullscreen Emergency crews and military personnel gather at the Wainwright Health Centre on Saturday. Photograph: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP

The country’s defence minister, David McGuinty, described the event as a “terrible incident” as he travelled to the scene to meet senior officials and first responders.

“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” he said, adding that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) were involved in the investigation.

McGuinty did not provide details about what caused the incident and the Canadian armed forces said on Sunday that its “immediate priority” was notifying next of kin and helping those affected by the fire. The armed forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, they said.

Canada’s top soldier, Gen Jennie Carignan, who serves as chief of the defence staff, called the incident “a profoundly difficult moment for the entire Canadian armed forces”.

View image in fullscreen The nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting support. Photograph: Jennifer Gauthier/Reuters

The nearby community of Wainwright provided hospital and firefighting support. Flares were spotted in the sky and military medical paratroopers dropped in on a local school football field.

Health staff in ‌Edmonton said a “code orange,” or mass-casualty ​event, was declared to coordinate ​the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright.

A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180km (112 miles) north-west of Wainwright, told Canada’s national broadcaster that Wainwright’s healthcare facilities had been inundated.

“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra hospital, told CBC News. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster.”

Officials asked people in Edmonton to avoid the emergency department at the University of Alberta hospital in order to prioritise victims from the military base. Air ambulances were dispatched from Saskatoon and Edmonton.

View image in fullscreen Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, said the nation was ‘in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost’. Photograph: Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press/AP

The fire at the military base swept into the area where the simulated attacks were taking place, crossing established firebreaks before being contained with help from municipal firefighters.

The Canadian military said there were no indications of terrorism.

On Sunday, the Alberta premier described the fire as “heartbreaking” and said it had affected many military personnel.

“On behalf of the government of Alberta, I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and wish those who have been injured a full recovery. Our thoughts are also with the military personnel, families and colleagues facing uncertainty and grief during this incredibly difficult time,” Smith said.

The premier said many of the injured would require “weeks and months” of specialised, intensive medical care. She is due to travel to meet senior officials in Edmonton.

The Saskatchewan premier, Scott Moe, said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

View image in fullscreen CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military bases. Photograph: Daphne Lemelin/AFP/Getty Images

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

“On behalf of the Nato military committee, we extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, and our wishes for a full recovery to all the injured,” Adm Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the chair of the Nato military committee, posted on social media. “Those who fell there served our common security, and the military committee will honour their memory.”

Canada’s Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, said he had spoken with Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.

“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

rss_8_1792447728.title: ‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile Argentina
rss_8_1792447728.text:
A dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.

Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors peered down on the scene.

The Falkland Islands, home to approximately 3,600 residents

Proceedings started at the raised hand of a bored-looking young man wearing headphones in the corner. He was transmitting the question and answer session via radio across the dozen or so inhabited islands that make up the 778-strong archipelago.

It was not clear how many of the Falklands’ 3,600 residents were listening in from their farm houses out in the diddle-dee shrub that coats much of the islands, or in the front rooms of Port Stanley’s white clapboard cottages with the pretty coloured roofs; likely not on a par with the number who learned 44 years ago from the Falkland Islands broadcasting station that their lands had been invaded.

“There’s no turning back, we can expect them by dawn,” the governor, Rex Hunt, had said then.

But for those who did tune in on Monday evening, there was much to dwell on. Not so much the answers about the local internet contract or the consultation on the contentious plan for a salmon farm.

“I have another one for you,” piped up one enthusiastic quizzer with a heavy local accent, a West Country burr with a slight antipodean lift. That intervention prompted a little shuffling of tired bums. But a rather more significant announcement was to come.

View image in fullscreen Assembly members Roger Spink, Stacy Bragger and Lewis Clifton before the monthly meeting.

Lewis Clifton, an assembly member who can date his family’s residence on the Falklands to the late 1870s, advised the islanders that an unprecedented economic war was being waged against them – a community no bigger than an English village – by a country of 46 million people.

“I am concerned that the level of Argentinian thrust this time has been at a different level,” Clifton said. “Perhaps a more vehement and belligerent tone than [seen since] 1982, because it has the potential to threaten our very economic development.”

Facing a downturn in his domestic polling and with an upcoming election, Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has legislated to criminalise companies and individuals involved in the Falklands’ nascent oil industry, and suggested the fisheries industry on which it currently relies for its prosperity could be next.

The British forces capability at Mount Pleasant airbase – 1,800 personnel there and on Ascension island, four typhoon jets, a ground-based air defence system and with HMS Medway patrolling the waters – makes a military threat from Argentina largely hypothetical. But Buenos Aires has launched a full spectrum attack of another sort.

View image in fullscreen Aerial view of a new port and floating jetty being built in the Falkland Islands.

In response this week, Andy Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, restated the UK’s solidarity with the islanders’ desire to remain British, and promised legislation that might offer some protection against the financial damage imposed by Argentina’s economic sanctions. Interpol received Foreign Office representations suggesting they reject an Argentinian request for arrests relating to the dispute.

For the islanders, it was a welcome show of muscularity. They have never felt entirely confident in the spine of those in power back on the homeland. It was arguably the indifference of Westminster that led Argentina to launch its invasion in the first place back in 1982.

“I have never trusted the Foreign Office and I have been proven right,” said Norma Edwards, 84, whose husband, Roger, 80, a former Royal Marine, was attached to the SAS in the 1982 conflict. “Catching up time,” said Clifton, of what he saw as a belated toughness from London this week. But things remain precarious.

View image in fullscreen Ricky Evans, who runs a guesthouse and other businesses, carries post and supplies for Pebble Island.

The Falkland Islands might be described as a British success story. Four decades ago, there were 1,800 inhabitants, and its tiny wool-centric economy, 300 miles (480km) east of mainland South America, was dependent on UK government handouts.

Today the population, growing at 3% year-on-year in recent times, includes about 70 different nationalities, attracted by the 26% top rate of tax, good pay and opportunities in a growing and entirely self-reliant economy.

There are Zimbabweans who came to de-mine after the war. Construction workers from South Africa who came to rebuild. Chileans who found something they liked after taking a Latam Airlines flight. The largest minority group is the Filipinos, who came to work in social care and the service industry in the late 1980s and 90s.

View image in fullscreen Chilean tourists pose for a photograph outside the Stanley post office.

Working behind the bar at Groovy’s, a Nepalese waiter said he had come from Dubai. The money was better in the Falklands, he said, and “the people are nicer”. “The locals start at Deano’s bar, then it’s the Victory bar and here – then it is the Globe, for dancing,” he said with a smile. “After that they go to house parties.”

Such has been the Falklands’ success in attracting people that a permanent residency scheme, capped at 90 people a year, has been frozen for 12 months. The islands, for all their challenges, are somewhere people want to be.

View image in fullscreen John Barton, chair of the Falkland Islands fishing companies association and James Bates, the executive secretary.

All of this had been made possible because of squid, said John Barton, chair of the fishing companies association. “It has been transformational,” he said.

In 1986, the UK allowed the Falklands to establish a 200-nautical-mile exclusive fishing zone in which those wanting to operate had to be licensed by the islands’ government. Licences sold to fleets of Spanish, Korean and Taiwanese “jiggers” have delivered major revenues, but the locals are increasingly running the vessels too.

The islands’ gross domestic production per capita soared as a result, from about £2,000 in 1982 to £85,000 in 2025, putting the islands sixth in the world league table, just behind Norway. The tourism industry is also going strong, with 75,000 or more people spilling out of cruise ships every year at Stanley port, but that is at best a nice addition.

View image in fullscreen James Wallace, who runs the Fortuna fishing company, onboard his harbour launch. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen A worker packs filleted toothfish into plastic bags at a Falkland Islands processing factory.

James Wallace, 41, is chief executive of Fortuna, the largest fishing company on the island. It is a growing operation, which last year acquired Cornwall’s oldest fishing business, the Ocean Fish Group. But he is diversifying his business for a reason.

The squid populations in the Falklands waters, on which his company and the islands rely, are hugely variable and it is clear that “catches are declining”, he said. “We have commissioned a bunch of inshore work to see what is happening but the answer is that we don’t yet know,” he said. But there is another natural resource on which the islanders’ hopes are pinned.

View image in fullscreen A bust of Margaret Thatcher by the 1982 war memorial.

About 136 miles north of the Falkland Islands, work is continuing at pace on the Sea Lion oil project led by Israeli firm Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration.

Independent estimates suggest the offshore oil field could triple the Falkland Islands’ GDP and deliver a Norway-style sovereign wealth fund. The companies involved remain confident that drilling will commence within months. A new jetty is busy with activity. But the impact of Argentinian pressure cannot be discounted. Two major contractors recently pulled out of the project.

View image in fullscreen Chief executive of the Falklands government, Andrea Clausen, in the room where Argentinian forces surrendered.

Andrea Clausen, as chief executive of the Falklands government, its top civil servant, works from a building on Thatcher Drive. Her office is opposite the room where Brig Gen Mario Menéndez signed Argentina’s letter of surrender on 14 June 1982. The letter remains on the wall.

Clausen was 10 at the time of the invasion and remembers the Argentinian solders’ arrival. She also recalls cowering with her family in their home in Goose Green, 60 miles west of Stanley, as the British Harrier jets came in with their cluster bombs. “Even now I struggle to cope with the sound of fast jets,” she said.

Clausen sees trauma throughout the islands. “I guess, some extreme behaviour,” she said. “Anger, aggression on certain political subjects.” She is evidently frustrated by the recent Argentinian actions.

“The Falklands has since [19]82 ensured that we are financially independent – save for defence,” she said. “We had no money in 82 and we never want to be in that position again.”

The oil is their insurance, she suggested. “I like to think that better people will de-escalate this because, honestly, we are 4,000 people minding our own business, we have a history deeper and older than theirs.”

View image in fullscreen Falkland Islands reserves (from left): Cpl Chris Stenning; Justin McPhee, director of emergency services; Lt Alastair Baylis; and warrant officer second class Paul Watson.

There are cycles to Argentinian bellicosity. The opportunistic but ill-fated invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator general Leopoldo Galtieri, leading to the death of 649 Argentinians and 255 British military personnel, along with three islanders, has cast a pall over Argentinian-UK relations ever since.

But at times, notably in the 1990s, Buenos Aires adopted a hearts-and-minds approach to the islanders, sending videos of the animated series Pingu to their children. Such kindness has tended to evaporate away, though, when an Argentinian government is losing public support at home, as Milei is experiencing now.

But if any one attribute sums up the islanders, it is resilience, said Dot Gould, an assembly member who owns Pebble, a 20-mile long island north-west of the Falklands. She and her husband share the island with a couple who run a lodge, 5,000 sheep, 100 cattle, a load of spectacular wildlife, but not much else.

View image in fullscreen Dot Gould, who owns Pebble island. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian

Rampaging around the undulating terrain in her 4x4 vehicle, avoiding colonies of Rockhopper and Gentoo penguins, Gould points out the scattered remains of an Argentinian fighter jet and the graves of two of the airmen killed during battle. As a child on Pebble, she used to play with the parachutes left by the Argentinians, using them as sails for a go-kart.

“I think, since 1982, this is probably the most serious it’s been for us,” she said. “How effective they will be, we don’t know yet … it’s almost two fingers up: we’ll get on with it, we have to.” But there is much that they want to do.

The islands are dependent on a narrow range of freight links from the UK and South America for much of their fresh produce. Any glitch, and peculiar shortages can emerge. There was a period without milk. A time without beer. During one cherry tomato shortage, which saw their price shoot up, the main supermarket opted to cut them in half and sell them like that to spread the joy.

A sorry-looking cabbage will set you back £8 at the West Store on the front. The local newspaper is the Penguin News (“This one’s not for Penguin News but …” is the traditional opening when disseminating islands gossip). But Facebook is the key means of communication. “Grown men and women use Snapchat like teenagers, often to arrange their extramarital affairs,” said one local.

View image in fullscreen Children during school lunch break.

Other peculiarities include the Falklands government paying for children from the age of 16 to complete their secondary and university education in the UK. The size of the islands’ population makes it impractical to offer such levels of education at home, said Sarah Stannard, the islands’ director of education.

But if the oil money comes online, she would rebuild the primary school. Children from the countryside – it is known locally as “camp” – are offered board in Stanley, although there are also peripatetic teachers and lessons done on the telephone.

The children grow up quickly here, and tend to be keen to broaden their horizons. Oliver Lee, 15, was keen to join the merchant navy. “I would like to see other places,” he said. “The Mediterranean, hotter places basically.” Layla-May Vatemanu, 14, said: “A lot of the boys especially in my class do a lot of sport. Our [friendship group] doesn’t have a lot to do.”

View image in fullscreen School students (from left): Oliver Lee, Layla May, Tessa Blake and Paul Green.

There are no bus services anywhere, and the more distant parts of the islands are only accessible via boat or the Falkland government’s twin-engine aircraft service. On a landmass half the size of Wales, there is only one cashpoint.

Touch rugby – rather than full-contact rugby – is played, in part because the islands’ hospital does not have the capability to deal with complex injuries. Much of the health budget goes on medi-evacs to South America. Yet, for all that, most of the children who leave at 16 do return.

All places are shaped by their history and geography, but some have more history and geography than others. “We are British with a twist,” said Stacy Bragger, a former journalist who represents the Stanley constituency in the assembly.

“We have our own identity. If you were to ask what are the traits of a Falkland islander – resourcefulness, resilience, making do. Because if something breaks you can’t just go down the road. You have to make do. That’s our version of Britishness.”

View image in fullscreen Mike Summers (left) and Liam Short, members of the chamber of commerce.

The islanders also have long memories. “I used to read the Guardian when I was a good deal younger,” said Mike Summers, 73, who sits on the board of the local chamber of commerce. “But I stopped reading it in 1982 when [the editor] Peter Preston just fucked me off so much. He was: ‘Oh well they are a long way away and there is only a few of them – so why don’t we just sell them?’”

On the Argentinian rhetoric, Summers added: “There are a lot of people who still suffer effects from the war – PTSD among the older people. I bumped into someone at the supermarket the other day who I have known for ever. She said: ‘Oh, I’m wondering if I should sell my house and move away. The Argies are going to invade again.’ It seriously affects some people and it is cruel actually.”

View image in fullscreen Social influencer Roxy King-Clark at her home in Stanley.

Roxy King-Clarke, 40, describes herself as the Falklands’ biggest influencer, with about 60,000 followers. She picked up a major following when posting in response to the Argentinian men’s football team brandishing a “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” [The Malvinas are Argentinian] banner at the World Cup.

She is regularly subjected to abuse for her posts. “The most common insults are to call us pirates, usurpers and colonisers,” she said. “It’s a bizarre thing to be on the receiving end of it all as they speak like we’ve just tipped up here. I can trace my family back to my earliest ancestor arriving here in 1842.”

Her generation too, she suggests, have taken lessons from what happened four decades ago. King-Clarke said she would take a “hard line” to avoid any misinterpretation. “We need to learn from history,” she said, “and not make the same mistakes.”

rss_9_1792447728.title: Mexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers​
rss_9_1792447728.text:
A Mexican ⁠judge ⁠has sentenced ​three men to 158 years ⁠and nine months in prison each for ⁠the murder of ​two Australian ‌brothers ‌and their American friend during ‌a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California.

The ‌defendants were declared guilty a week ​ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft ⁠with violence, crimes committed against ​Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad.

Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in a suspected robbery while travelling through Mexico.

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on 27 April 2024.

Their bodies were found days later in a clifftop well with gunshot wounds to the heads.

Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons.

Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have been sentenced.

The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link.

View image in fullscreen Debra and Martin Robinson, parents of Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson, during a news conference outside court after the verdict. Photograph: Karen Castaneda/AP

Prosecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings.

The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.

They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.

Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups.

Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia.

He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.
